newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-OWNERS REJECT PROPOSED LABOR AGREEMENT.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-OWNERS REJECT PROPOSED LABOR AGREEMENT.

text.p: Baseball owners rejected a proposed labour agreement by a surprisingly large margin on Wednesday and voted unanimously to use their executive council in further negotiations with players.

Just 12 of the 30 owners, including the two expansion clubs that have yet to play, voted in favour of the labour deal reached by management negotiatior Randy Levine and union chief Donald Fehr during the World Series last month.
Acting commissioner Bud Selig, owner of the Milwaukee Brewers, denied the two sides were back where they started in 1993.

"This is not going back to square one," he said. "Most of the elements of the deal that Randy and Donald Fehr negotiated are agreeable to the majority of owners. What we need are some modifications in a couple of very important areas."

Selig said during the World Series that a deal had to be reached by November 15 for interleague play to take place in 1997 as planned. November 15 is also the date that free agents can begin signing with new teams.

"I assume there will be a cut-off date to have a schedule with interleague play," Selig said Wednesday. "We will negotiate hard with the union in the next week or 10 days to try and get this deal completed."
The proposal would have set a luxury tax of 35 percent on payrolls exceeding $51 million in 1997, with the threshold escalating to nearly $59 million by 1999.
While Selig refused to give specifics, there were indications that owners want the proposed luxury tax in place for 2000 and 2001, the last two years of the proposed deal.
The proposal for no luxury tax in those years could be a major sticking point with the players' union -- and among the owners themselves.

Owners of small-market clubs say they cannot compete against richer franchises without a tax on the big-money teams to slow their spending and fund their poorer cousins. Players object to restrictions on their ability to seek the highest pay the market will bear.

Selig, himself the owner of a small-market club, has pointed out that the World Series this year was won by the richest team in baseball, the Yankees, playing against the highest-payroll team in the National League, the Braves.
The 12-member Executive Council consists of Selig, American League President Gene Budig, National League President Leonard Coleman and nine owners.

The owners are Minnesota's Carl Pohlad, Boston's John Harrington, Jerry Reinsdorf of the Chicago White Sox, George Steinbrenner of the New York Yankees, Montreal's Claude Brouchu, Philadelphia's Bill Giles, Colorado's Jerry McMorris, Fred Wilpon of the New York Mets and the Atlanta Braves' Bill Bartholomay.
"We feel confident that the Executive Council can pick up where Randy Levine and Donald Fehr left off and get a good deal for both sides," said Reinsdorf, a leader of the hardline wing of the owners.
When asked if the council would require a unanimous vote to ratify any deal, Selig said, "I would like a unanimous vote, but a simple majority would be enough."
Selig tried to head off speculation that Levine would no longer have a hand in the negotiations.

"As far as I know, Randy is going to continue to be the negotiator with us," Selig said. "Everyone on the council will be negotiators. But I will talk to Randy tomorrow (Thursday) and get his feelings."

The owners began voting in the early evening after Levine gave them the proposal. In addition to the 28 current teams, owners for the expansion Arizona Diamondbacks and Tampa Bay Devil Rays also participated.
Players have already voted to give their union's executive board the authority to ratify a contract.
Players and owners have been without an agreement since December 31, 1993.

The players struck in 1994 when the owners tried to impose a salary cap, and the owners cancelled the remainder of the 1994 season in September, wiping out the World Series for the first time since 1904 and knocking 18 games off the start of the 1995 season.

The strike ended following a March 31, 1995, injunction issued by United States District Court Judge Sonya Sotomayor, who ordered baseball to play under the bylaws of its previous collective bargaining agreement.
